questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f: \mathbb{R} - \{-3\} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x+3}$. Show that $f$ is bijective. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A function is bijective if it is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto its stated codomain).

**The function is well defined.** For $x \ne -3$, $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x+3}$ exists, and $f(x) \ne 1$ because $\dfrac{x}{x+3} = 1 \Rightarrow x = x + 3 \Rightarrow 0 = 3$, impossible. So $f$ really maps $\mathbb{R} - \{-3\}$ into $\mathbb{R} - \{1\}$.

**Injective.** Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R} - \{-3\}$ with $f(a) = f(b)$.

$$\frac{a}{a+3} = \frac{b}{b+3} \Longrightarrow a(b+3) = b(a+3) \Longrightarrow ab + 3a = ab + 3b \Longrightarrow 3a = 3b \Longrightarrow a = b.$$

So $f$ is injective.

**Surjective.** Let $y \in \mathbb{R} - \{1\}$. We look for $x$ with $f(x) = y$:

$$\frac{x}{x+3} = y \Longrightarrow x = y(x + 3) \Longrightarrow x - yx = 3y \Longrightarrow x(1 - y) = 3y \Longrightarrow x = \frac{3y}{1 - y}.$$

This is defined because $y \ne 1$. It also belongs to the domain, i.e. $x \ne -3$: if $\dfrac{3y}{1-y} = -3$ then $3y = -3 + 3y$, i.e. $0 = -3$, impossible. Substituting back: $f\!\left(\dfrac{3y}{1-y}\right) = \dfrac{3y/(1-y)}{3y/(1-y) + 3} = \dfrac{3y}{3y + 3(1-y)} = \dfrac{3y}{3} = y$. So every $y\in\mathbb{R} - \{1\}$ has a preimage: $f$ is surjective.

Since $f$ is injective and surjective, $f$ is bijective, with inverse $f^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{3y}{1-y}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the periodic function $f$ with period $6$, where
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} x - 2, & 2 \le x \le 5,\\[2pt] -\tfrac12 x + 4, & 5 < x \le 8,\end{cases}$$
show that $f$ is not continuous at $x = 5$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A function is continuous at $x = 5$ only if $\lim_{x\to5^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to5^+} f(x) = f(5)$.

- Value at $5$ (first rule, since $5 \in [2, 5]$): $f(5) = 5 - 2 = 3$.
- Left-hand limit (first rule, for $x < 5$): $\lim_{x\to5^-}(x - 2) = 3$.
- Right-hand limit (second rule, for $x > 5$): $\lim_{x\to5^+}\left(-\tfrac12 x + 4\right) = -\tfrac52 + 4 = \tfrac32$.

The left-hand limit $3$ and the right-hand limit $\tfrac32$ are different, so $\lim_{x\to5} f(x)$ does not exist (the graph has a jump of $\tfrac32$ at $x = 5$). Therefore $f$ is not continuous at $x = 5$. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the periodic function $f$ with period $6$, where
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} x - 2, & 2 \le x \le 5,\\[2pt] -\tfrac12 x + 4, & 5 < x \le 8,\end{cases}$$
find $f(19)$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The rule is given on $[2, 8]$, an interval of length $6$ (the period). Since $f(x + 6) = f(x)$, subtract multiples of $6$ from $19$ until the value lies in $[2, 8]$:

$$f(19) = f(19 - 6) = f(13) = f(13 - 6) = f(7).$$

(Subtracting $18$ would give $1$, which is outside $[2, 8]$, so we stop at $7$.) Now $7 \in (5, 8]$, so the second rule applies:

$$f(7) = -\tfrac12(7) + 4 = -3.5 + 4 = 0.5.$$

$$\boxed{f(19) = \tfrac12}$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the periodic function $f$ with period $6$, where
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} x - 2, & 2 \le x \le 5,\\[2pt] -\tfrac12 x + 4, & 5 < x \le 8,\end{cases}$$
sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$ in the interval $-1 \le x \le 8$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Part of the graph already given, $2 \le x \le 8$.**

- On $[2, 5]$: $y = x - 2$, a straight line of gradient $1$ from $(2, 0)$ to $(5, 3)$. The end $(5, 3)$ is a **closed** dot (included).
- On $(5, 8]$: $y = -\tfrac12 x + 4$, a straight line of gradient $-\tfrac12$ from $(5, \tfrac32)$ to $(8, 0)$. The point $(5, \tfrac32)$ is an **open** circle (excluded) and $(8, 0)$ is a closed dot. This is the jump found in part (a).

**Part obtained by periodicity, $-1 \le x \le 2$.** For $x$ in this interval, $x + 6 \in [5, 8]$ and $f(x) = f(x+6)$.

- For $-1 < x \le 2$: $x + 6 \in (5, 8]$, so $f(x) = -\tfrac12(x + 6) + 4 = 1 - \tfrac12 x$. This is a line of gradient $-\tfrac12$ through $(0, 1)$ and ending at $(2, 0)$, where it joins the line $y = x - 2$ continuously ($f(2) = 0$). At $x = -1$ the line starts at the **open** circle $(-1, \tfrac32)$.
- At $x = -1$: $f(-1) = f(5) = 3$, so there is a **closed** dot at $(-1, 3)$.

**Key points to mark.**

| $x$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $2$ | $5$ | $5^+$ | $8$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f(x)$ | $3$ (closed), $\tfrac32$ (open, from the right) | $1$ | $0$ | $3$ (closed) | $\tfrac32$ (open) | $0$ |

**Shape.** A saw-tooth with period $6$: starting at the closed dot $(-1, 3)$, a gap, then a descending segment from the open circle $(-1, \tfrac32)$ through $(0, 1)$ to $(2, 0)$; an ascending segment from $(2, 0)$ to the closed dot $(5, 3)$; a gap, then a descending segment from the open circle $(5, \tfrac32)$ to the closed dot $(8, 0)$. The pattern between $x = -1$ and $x = 5$ is identical to the pattern between $x = 5$ and $x = 11$, which confirms the period of $6$. The graph lies between $y = 0$ and $y = 3$.
